Hypernetwork for LoRA Weights Unlike steering vectors, LoRA adapters condition their update on the layer input x x rather than adding a constant offset, so the intervention varies with what the model is writing. Therefore, we extend the previous setup to predict LoRA weights, inspired by Charakorn et al. (2025) which predicts LoRA weights given novel task descriptions. (4) The module initialization mirrors standard LoRA, where the 𝐀 \mathbf{A} -heads are initialized with zero weights and uniform biases, and the 𝐁 \mathbf{B} -heads with zero weights and biases. This leaves the adapters as a no-op at initialization and was essential for training stability in our case. We treat the set of adapted layers as a design choice, restricting it to a middle-layer subset as it acts as a regularizer and improves downstream metrics ( Table 5 ). Training As shown in Figure 1 , both learned steering and the hypernetworks are trained end-to-end with the author’s ground-truth abstract. The base model and the encoder stay frozen, and gradients pass through M M into the prediction network alone. Crucially, M M receives the zero-shot prompt: the references never enter its context, so style is carried entirely by the predicted parameters. 5 Experimental Setup 5.1 Data Creation Source and Filtering Our dataset is built from an arXiv snapshot. We retain papers with permissive licenses 2 2 2 Some licenses require mentioning the authors. We include this in our repository (deanonymized upon publication). in the cs.AI and cs.LG categories. Publication year is capped at 2022, so that ground-truth abstracts cannot have been written by a modern LLM: the style targets are guaranteed human . Lacking unique author identifiers, we treat identical author names as one person and discard authors publishing in over five arXiv categories as a disambiguation heuristic. We assume the first author is a paper’s primary writer. Papers without parsable L a T e X source or an introduction are excluded. Outline Creation As defined in § 3 , the models receive an outline rather than the full paper. This ensures that minimal style information is available in the input. We clean the L a T e X source to plain text and prompt Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 to produce bullet points under four headings: Context, Methodology, Results, and Conclusion. Additional details and prompts are in Appendix A.3 . Statistics After filtering, the dataset contains 1,232 papers from 203 authors, averaging 6.07 papers each (range 5-14). One paper per author forms the validation set and one the test set, and the remaining 826 form the training set. Each entry pairs a paper’s outline with its ground-truth abstract, its introduction, and three abstracts sampled randomly from the same author’s remaining papers. Unseen Author Test Set To evaluate generalization, we create a second test set where none of the authors appeared in training for either the generation models or the author classifier. In this set, the authors have exactly four papers, which guarantees disjointness from the base dataset. It contains 1,312 papers from 328 authors: three per author serve as prompt examples and one as the test sample. 5.2 Baselines We compare our methods to three standard ones, with the corresponding prompts in Appendix A.4 . Zero-Shot The base model generates an abstract from the outline alone. It receives no author information, and therefore provides a lower bound on style accuracy and a quality anchor. Few-Shot The zero-shot prompt is extended with the three reference abstracts, and the model is instructed to extract and apply the author’s style. This measures style transfer without parameter updates. LoRA The base model is fine-tuned on the few-shot prompt with adapters on the query and value projections at rank r = 8 r=8 , matching the hypernetwork’s adapter budget so that the two are directly comparable. It represents the strongest style baseline. Note that here LoRA is not per-author , as our data only contain roughly five abstracts per author. Instead, a single set of LoRA adapters is optimized across all training authors and conditioned at inference on the three author-specific examples. 5.3 Implementation Details All models use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 Qwen Team (2025) as the frozen base model M M (36 layers, d = 2,560 d=2{,}560 ). We decode with sampling ( T = 0.7 T=0.7 , repetition penalty 1.05 1.05 , top- p = 0.8 p=0.8 , top- k = 20 k=20 ) and generate 1,024 tokens at most. The k k NN author classifier is a fine-tuned distilbert-base-uncased with k = 3 k=3 and cosine distance. Both learned steering and the hypernetwork use a four-block MLP backbone with an author representation of 128 dimensions. Configuration searches use the validation set, while the test set is reserved for final evaluation. Manual steering uses our contrast method at layers 18-20 with λ = 0.875 \lambda=0.875 . Learned steering encodes the three example abstracts with the STAR encoder Huertas-Tato et al. (2024) and predicts a shift vector for all 36 layers. The hypernetwork uses the same STAR encoder and predicts rank-8 adapters for the query and value projections, matching the LoRA baseline’s rank. Table 3: Style and quality results on two tests sets with (a) seen and (b) unseen authors. 6.2 Results on Seen Authors 3a reports test set results for our three approaches alongside the three baselines and the ground truth, evaluated on the 203 authors seen during training. We report preference rate as the primary quality metric and author classifier accuracy as the primary style metric. All models preserve the paper’s topic at comparable levels (95.6-97.5%), which is a precondition for comparing style accuracy rather than a discriminating result. Few-shot baseline fails to convey author style. The few-shot baseline scores below the zero-shot baseline on both style metrics (28.1% and 0.36 against 31.0% and 0.40), despite receiving the same examples the LoRA baseline is trained with. It thus falls below the content-only reference point, potentially because instruction-following pulls the output toward a generic instructed register, moving embeddings away from any specific author. Quality degrades as well (91.5% preference rate). Direct fine-tuning maximizes style at the cost of quality. The LoRA setup attains the highest style accuracy at 49.8%, roughly 84% of the range above the content-only reference point. However, its preference rate falls drastically to 38.1% from 97.9% for the zero-shot baseline, so fine-tuning purchases nearly all of the available style signal by sacrificing what makes the abstracts usable. Manual inspection reveals fluency issues with frequent repetitions. Activation steering preserves quality but yields small gains. Both steering approaches improve style while leaving quality largely intact. Manual steering reaches 34.5% at a preference rate of 94.3%, the highest of any model improving on the zero-shot style accuracy, and the prediction network reaches 35.0% at 89.6%. Predicting vectors therefore matches hand-computed ones on style without a neutral generation per reference or a search over intensity. The two differ by a single abstract, and § 7.1 shows they achieve this by steering in nearly orthogonal directions. Hypernet LoRA balances style and quality. The hypernetwork LoRA reaches 36.5%, roughly a quarter of the range, while retaining a preference rate of 91.3% that direct fine-tuning forfeits. Both amortize across authors rather than fitting each separately, differing in that LoRA carries style through the context window with a shared adapter, whereas the hypernetwork carries it through adapter weights predicted per author. Note the two methods are matched on adapter budget but not on information: LoRA reads the example text directly and can copy surface phrasing, while the hypernetwork conditions only on their embeddings. 6.3 Generalization to Unseen Authors So far, the models were tested on authors present in the training data. We now assess if style conditioning transfers to authors that neither the models nor the author classifier have seen ( 3b ). Model rankings are preserved. Every value is lower than on the seen authors, including the ground truth (41.5% against 53.2%). Only the relative ordering is informative, and it is identical, with few-shot again last and below the zero-shot baseline. As the seen and unseen sets share no authors, generation noise is an implausible explanation for the few-shot result. Hypernet retains position. The hypernetwork improves style by 8.5 points over the zero-shot baseline while giving up 1.9 points of preference rate, ranking second on all three metrics, and the standard LoRA setup again buys the highest style accuracy at a preference rate of 39.0%. The trade-off structure thus reappears unchanged on authors no component of the system was trained on. The hypernetwork now recovers close to half of the range against roughly 79% for LoRA, where the seen-author fractions were a quarter and 84%, though the narrower unseen range inflates these fractions and they are not directly comparable across sets. The hypernetwork sits immediately before quality degrades. 6.4 Style-Quality Trade-Off Figure 2 plots preference rate against style accuracy. We characterize the trade-off by Pareto dominance on point estimates. Three models are Pareto-optimal: the zero-shot baseline on preference rate, LoRA on style accuracy, and the hypernetwork LoRA between them. On the seen authors the frontier also contains manual steering, so the hypernetwork is the only one of our approaches Pareto-optimal on both sets at the configurations of 3a . Two qualifications apply. First, the two learned methods are reported at different intervention scopes: learned steering over all 36 layers and the hypernetwork over layers 18–20. At the common scope 18–20 ( Table 5 ), the hypernetwork retains higher style accuracy (36.5% vs. 34.0%) but learned steering attains the higher preference rate (97.5% vs. 91.3%), so neither dominates and the seen-set frontier is scope-dependent. Second, several style-accuracy differences correspond to few examples; manual and predicted steering differ by a single abstract on the seen-author test set. We therefore report paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals in 3a and read Pareto statements as descriptive of point estimates rather than as significance claims. Relative to the hypernetwork, on the unseen set, LoRA buys 6.1 points of style accuracy for 56.5 points of preference rate.
